Hello everyone! My husband and I have a very young but sizable family. Our children are quite young. I understand that extensive hiking isn't something that will be happening very soon for our family since the kids are so small. When we go for an evening walk, we still have to keep at a toddler's pace.

In the coming years, I'd like to take family day trips or overnight trips to interesting local areas of interest. We live in the upper midwest, USA, and there are so many beautiful places in our state that I'd love to go see and share with my family. I want to encourage curiosity, exploration, exercise, and fitness in my children as they grow.

What are some ways that you have found helpful to incorporate young children in hikes? Is there information that is available about what are good distances for each age? When I'm researching places to go, what are clues on the locations' websites that it would be a good or bad place to take young children?

Is there any other information that you can think of that I should know when you read this? We've been pretty sedentary for a long time, and I want to change everything about that. I'm hoping to turn our family from homebodies into camping/hiking/biking explorers. I'm not sure I know what questions to ask.

edit: Changed identifying details.
What is the best way to get my family started to become a hiking family?

This is wonderful. did this a lot when the kids were little. Start small, with stuff that looks special and fun to them. If you have a zoo, it's a great place to start walking. Parks. Then wild places, but not too far out; then more special places. Not too hilly, and NOT in hot weather. Little ones really don't do well in hot weather, or extremely cold weather.
Hiking is one of the most wonderful pastimes in the world. So is bicycling. Which we also did. Best wishes & I hope you have a wonderful time.

Start taking family walks before/after dinner. Getting a good system down for who does what when walking is critical so the children know what they should be doing when you're in unfamiliar territory.

I can see how a system would be important. We went out for a walk last night, and our oldest kept running ahead. It was a struggle to get him to stay with the group. This is going to be a crazy undertaking, but I'm excited about it. :)

The easiest way to make sure your kids enjoy hiking is for you to truly enjoy it. When you go, don't keep focusing on how far you still have to go, slow down and take everything in. There's so many people that it seems like they don't actually enjoy hiking, they like the idea of being hikers, if that makes sense. Hiking is a blast, it's addicting, but not if you're just focused on getting back to the car the whole time.

Enjoy the view at the top. There's nothing better than resting with a hikers' high at a scenic overlook.

Definitely. This is a good point. I want to do it not only to be active, but to get my kids out in nature and learn about it. I thought about making it fun for them by giving them a list of items they need to find, and taking some local plant and bird books too so we can identify the things we see.

My oldest son is very interested in birds, and I'd like to foster that even though I know next to nothing about the different kinds of them. Plus it's so important to know about the plants to prevent poisoning, etc.

I figured hiking would be one of the best all-encompassing learning experiences there can be. :D It could be like family time/Montessori school. Lol, I worry I'm being too ambitious with these thoughts.
